solution:
(i) **1-Phenylethanol from a suitable alkene.** Acid-catalysed hydration of styrene follows Markovnikov's rule, because protonation at the terminal carbon gives the resonance-stabilised benzylic carbocation:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_3\)

(ii) **Cyclohexylmethanol by an \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) reaction.** The halide must be primary; chloromethylcyclohexane is hydrolysed by aqueous alkali, hydroxide attacking the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{NaCl}\)

(iii) **Pentan-1-ol from a suitable alkyl halide.** Again a primary halide is required:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{NaBr}\)

Two reactions showing that phenol is acidic:
1. With an active metal, liberating hydrogen:
\(2\,\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2\,\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2\)
2. With aqueous sodium hydroxide, forming a salt:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

**Comparison with ethanol.** Phenol is the far stronger acid; \(\text{p}K_a\) is about 10.0 for phenol against 15.9 for ethanol, a difference of roughly \(10^6\) in \(K_a\). Two reasons:
- In the phenoxide ion the negative charge is **delocalised** over the ring by resonance, being shared with the two ortho and the para carbons, so the anion is strongly stabilised. In the ethoxide ion the charge stays localised on one oxygen atom.
- The \(-\text{OH}\) group of phenol is bonded to an \(sp^2\) carbon, which is more electronegative than the \(sp^3\) carbon of ethanol and withdraws electron density, increasing the polarity of the O\(-\)H bond. In ethanol the alkyl group is electron releasing (\(+I\)), which pushes electron density on to oxygen and makes the proton harder to remove.

The difference is decisive enough that phenol dissolves in aqueous NaOH whereas ethanol does not react with it.

The acidity of a phenol is governed by how well the phenoxide ion left after losing the proton is stabilised.

In **ortho-nitrophenol** the \(-\text{NO}_2\) group is strongly electron withdrawing, both inductively (\(-I\)) and by resonance (\(-R\)). Because it is ortho to the \(-\text{O}^-\), the negative charge that resonance places on that ring carbon can be delocalised one step further, on to the electronegative oxygen atoms of the nitro group. The anion is therefore extensively stabilised and the proton is lost readily.

In **ortho-methoxyphenol** the \(-\text{OCH}_3\) group carries lone pairs on oxygen and is electron **releasing** by resonance (\(+R\)). Donating electron density into the ring intensifies the negative charge already present on the phenoxide oxygen, which destabilises the anion. (Its weak \(-I\) effect is far outweighed by this \(+R\) donation.)

A more stable conjugate base means a stronger acid, so ortho-nitrophenol is more acidic than ortho-methoxyphenol — indeed methoxyphenol is a weaker acid even than phenol itself.

Electrophilic substitution requires the ring to supply electrons to the electrophile, so anything that raises the electron density of the ring activates it.

The oxygen of the \(-\text{OH}\) group carries lone pairs in a \(p\) orbital that can overlap with the \(\pi\) system of the ring. Delocalisation of one lone pair into the ring gives canonical structures in which the oxygen becomes positive and a **negative charge appears on the ortho and para carbons**:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \leftrightarrow\) structures with \(\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{H}\) and the negative charge at C-2, C-4 and C-6.

Two consequences follow:
- The ring as a whole is electron richer than benzene, so it attacks electrophiles faster — the group is **activating**.
- The extra electron density sits specifically at the ortho and para positions, so the electrophile adds there; the arenium ion formed by ortho or para attack has an additional canonical structure in which the oxygen's lone pair supplies the positive carbon a complete octet, which is the most stable of all the contributing structures. Hence \(-\text{OH}\) is **ortho, para directing** as well as activating.

This is why phenol brominates without a Lewis-acid catalyst and gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol with bromine water.

(i) Alkaline \(\text{KMnO}_4\) is a strong oxidising agent, so the primary alcohol is oxidised right through to the acid (isolated as its salt, and liberated on acidification):
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{alk. KMnO}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^- \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}\)
(propanoic acid)

(ii) In a solvent of low polarity such as \(\text{CS}_2\), and at low temperature, only one bromine enters:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{Br}_2 \xrightarrow[273\ \text{K}]{\text{CS}_2} o\text{-bromophenol (minor)} + p\text{-bromophenol (major)} + \text{HBr}\)

(iii) With dilute nitric acid at low temperature phenol is mononitrated at the ortho and para positions:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{HNO}_3(\text{dil.}) \rightarrow o\text{-nitrophenol} + p\text{-nitrophenol} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(iv) This is the Reimer-Tiemann reaction; chloroform and alkali generate dichlorocarbene, which attacks the ortho position, and the intermediate is hydrolysed:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{CHCl}_3 + \text{aq. NaOH}} o\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHCl}_2 \xrightarrow[\text{then H}^+]{\text{NaOH}} o\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHO}\)
(salicylaldehyde)

(i) **Kolbe's reaction.** Phenol is converted by alkali into the phenoxide ion, which is more nucleophilic than phenol itself; carbon dioxide, a weak electrophile, then substitutes at the ortho position and acidification gives salicylic acid:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} \xrightarrow{\text{CO}_2} o\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COONa} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} o\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-COOH}\)

(ii) **Reimer-Tiemann reaction.** Chloroform in aqueous sodium hydroxide generates dichlorocarbene \(:\text{CCl}_2\), which attacks the phenoxide ring at the ortho position; hydrolysis of the resulting benzal chloride gives salicylaldehyde:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{CHCl}_3,\ \text{aq. NaOH}} o\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CHO}\)

(iii) **Williamson ether synthesis.** An alkyl halide is treated with a sodium alkoxide or aryloxide; the alkoxide attacks the carbon of the halide by \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\), so the halide should be primary:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{ONa} + \text{CH}_3\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OCH}_3 + \text{NaBr}\)

(iv) **Unsymmetrical (mixed) ether.** An ether \(\text{R}-\text{O}-\text{R}'\) in which the two groups attached to oxygen are different, for example ethoxybenzene \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{O}-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\) or methoxyethane \(\text{CH}_3-\text{O}-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\). (Contrast a symmetrical ether such as ethoxyethane \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5-\text{O}-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\).)

Dehydration of ethanol with concentrated sulphuric acid at 443 K proceeds in three steps.

**Step 1 — formation of the protonated alcohol** (fast). The lone pair on the oxygen picks up a proton, converting \(-\text{OH}\) into \(-\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{H}_2\), which is a much better leaving group:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{H}^+ \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{H}_2\)

**Step 2 — formation of the carbocation** (slow; this is the rate-determining step). Water departs:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

**Step 3 — loss of a proton from the adjacent carbon**, giving the alkene:
\(\text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 + \text{H}^+\)

The proton taken up in step 1 is returned in step 3, so the acid is a catalyst. All three steps are reversible; the equilibrium is driven to the right by removing ethene as it is formed.

(i) **Propene \(\rightarrow\) propan-2-ol.** Acid-catalysed hydration, which follows Markovnikov's rule because the secondary carbocation is the more stable:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{OH})\text{CH}_3\)

(ii) **Benzyl chloride \(\rightarrow\) benzyl alcohol.** Hydrolysis with aqueous alkali:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH(aq)} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{NaCl}\)

(iii) **Ethyl magnesium chloride \(\rightarrow\) propan-1-ol.** A Grignard reagent with methanal gives a primary alcohol one carbon longer:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{MgCl} + \text{HCHO} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OMgCl} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)

(iv) **Methyl magnesium bromide \(\rightarrow\) 2-methylpropan-2-ol.** A Grignard reagent with a ketone gives a tertiary alcohol; propanone supplies the other two methyl groups:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{MgBr} + \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{OMgBr} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+} (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{OH}\)

(i) Acidified potassium permanganate (or \(\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\)) — a strong oxidising agent, which carries the primary alcohol past the aldehyde to the carboxylic acid.
(ii) Pyridinium chlorochromate, PCC (chromium trioxide with pyridine and HCl); \(\text{CrO}_3\) in an anhydrous medium also works. Being mild and water free, it stops at the aldehyde.
(iii) Bromine water, \(\text{Br}_2\) in \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) — the polar medium promotes polybromination, and 2,4,6-tribromophenol separates as a white precipitate.
(iv) Acidified \(\text{KMnO}_4\) (alkaline \(\text{KMnO}_4\) followed by acidification serves equally well).
(v) Concentrated \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) with heating (85% \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4\) at about 440 K is the milder alternative) — acid-catalysed dehydration.
(vi) Sodium borohydride, \(\text{NaBH}_4\) (\(\text{LiAlH}_4\), or \(\text{H}_2\) over Ni, also reduce the ketone).

Ethanol \((\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})\) and methoxymethane \((\text{CH}_3\text{OCH}_3)\) are isomers, both of molecular mass 46, so their dispersion forces are essentially the same.

Ethanol possesses an \(\text{O}-\text{H}\) bond. The hydrogen is bonded to a highly electronegative oxygen and is therefore able to form **intermolecular hydrogen bonds** with the lone pair of a neighbouring molecule, so ethanol exists as an associated liquid.

Methoxymethane has both hydrogens on carbon; it has no \(\text{O}-\text{H}\) bond, so although its C\(-\)O bonds are polar and give the molecule a small dipole moment, its molecules can only attract one another by weak dipole\(-\)dipole and dispersion forces. Ether oxygen can accept a hydrogen bond but cannot donate one, so ether molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other.

More energy is needed to separate hydrogen-bonded ethanol molecules, so ethanol boils much higher (351 K) than methoxymethane (248 K).

In every case the sodium alkoxide (or aryloxide) is made from the corresponding alcohol/phenol with sodium, and it then displaces halide from a **primary** alkyl halide by \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\).

(i) **1-Propoxypropane.** Reagents: sodium propoxide and 1-bromopropane.
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{ONa} + \text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{NaBr}\)

(ii) **Ethoxybenzene.** Reagents: sodium phenoxide and bromoethane. The aryl group must be supplied as the phenoxide, since bromobenzene cannot undergo \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\).
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{ONa} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{O}-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{NaBr}\)

(iii) **2-Methoxy-2-methylpropane.** Reagents: sodium tert-butoxide and bromomethane. The bulky group must come from the alkoxide; using methoxide with tert-butyl bromide would give 2-methylpropene by elimination instead.
\((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CONa} + \text{CH}_3\text{Br} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{O}-\text{CH}_3 + \text{NaBr}\)

(iv) **1-Methoxyethane (methoxyethane).** Reagents: sodium methoxide and bromoethane (or sodium ethoxide and bromomethane — both partners are primary, so either combination works).
\(\text{CH}_3\text{ONa} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{O}-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{NaBr}\)

Williamson synthesis is an \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) displacement, and this dictates its limitations.

**1. Secondary and tertiary alkyl halides fail.** An alkoxide is not only a nucleophile but also a strong base. With a hindered halide the rear-side approach needed for substitution is blocked, so the alkoxide instead removes a \(\beta\)-hydrogen and elimination takes over. With a tertiary halide no ether at all is obtained:
\((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{Br} + \text{CH}_3\text{ONa} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{CH}_3\text{OH} + \text{NaBr}\)
The remedy is to reverse the roles — use the tertiary alkoxide with a primary halide:
\((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CONa} + \text{CH}_3\text{Br} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{OCH}_3 + \text{NaBr}\)

**2. Aryl halides cannot be used.** The halogen is on an \(sp^2\) carbon and the C\(-\)X bond has partial double-bond character through resonance, so it is short, strong and not open to rear-side attack. Anisole therefore cannot be made from bromobenzene and sodium methoxide; it must be made from sodium phenoxide and bromomethane.

In short, the alkyl halide should always be primary, and where one group is aryl or tertiary it must be introduced as the alkoxide/aryloxide.

1-Propoxypropane is obtained by the bimolecular acid dehydration of propan-1-ol — that is, heating the alcohol with concentrated sulphuric acid at a moderate temperature (about 413 K; a higher temperature would give propene instead):
\(2\,\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow[413\ \text{K}]{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

**Mechanism** (nucleophilic bimolecular, \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\)):

**Step 1 — protonation.** The alcohol oxygen accepts a proton, turning \(-\text{OH}\) into the good leaving group \(-\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{H}_2\):
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{H}^+ \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{H}_2\)

**Step 2 — \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) attack.** A second, unprotonated molecule of propan-1-ol uses a lone pair on its oxygen to attack the carbon bearing the oxonium group, displacing water:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\ddot{\text{O}}\text{H} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\text{O}}(\text{H})-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

**Step 3 — deprotonation**, which regenerates the catalyst:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\overset{+}{\text{O}}(\text{H})-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}^+\)

The method succeeds here because propan-1-ol is primary and unhindered, so substitution outruns elimination.

Acid dehydration makes an ether by an \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) attack of one alcohol molecule on another that has been protonated. Two things go wrong when the alcohol is secondary or tertiary.

**Steric hindrance.** The carbon carrying the \(-\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{H}_2\) group already bears two or three alkyl groups, which shield it from rear-side approach. The bimolecular substitution therefore becomes very slow.

**Competing elimination.** Secondary and especially tertiary alcohols lose water readily to give relatively stable secondary and tertiary carbocations. Once such a carbocation exists it loses a \(\beta\)-proton far faster than it is captured by a bulky alcohol molecule, so elimination (E1) wins and an alkene is formed:
\((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{OH} \xrightarrow[358\ \text{K}]{20\%\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4} (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

So the reaction gives alkenes rather than ethers, and the method is confined to unhindered primary alcohols. Ethers with a secondary or tertiary group are instead made by Williamson synthesis, using that group as the alkoxide.

Hydrogen iodide protonates the ether oxygen; iodide then attacks whichever carbon can accept it most easily — the less hindered carbon in an \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) sense, or a carbon able to bear a stabilised positive charge.

(i) **1-Propoxypropane.** The ether is symmetrical and both groups are primary, so a single pair of products is obtained:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{HI} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{I} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)
(with excess HI the propan-1-ol is converted to 1-iodopropane as well).

(ii) **Methoxybenzene (anisole).** The aryl\(-\)O bond is not broken, because its \(sp^2\) carbon has partial double-bond character and cannot undergo nucleophilic substitution; attack occurs at the methyl carbon:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{OCH}_3 + \text{HI} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{I} + \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}\)
The phenol formed does not react further with HI for the same reason.

(iii) **Benzyl ethyl ether.** The benzylic carbocation is resonance stabilised by the ring, so cleavage occurs at the benzylic carbon:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2-\text{O}-\text{C}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{HI} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{I} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}\)

Both effects follow from the ability of the alkoxy oxygen to share a lone pair with the ring.

**(i) Activation.** A lone pair in a \(p\) orbital on oxygen overlaps with the \(\pi\) system of the benzene ring, so electron density flows from oxygen into the ring (a \(+R\) effect). Canonical structures can be written in which the oxygen bears a positive charge and a negative charge appears in the ring. The ring is thus made electron richer than benzene itself and attacks an electrophile more readily; the alkoxy group is strongly activating. This outweighs the \(-I\) effect of the electronegative oxygen, which acts in the opposite sense. It is why anisole is brominated by bromine in ethanoic acid without any iron(III) bromide catalyst.

**(ii) Ortho, para direction.** The delocalisation does not spread the charge evenly. Writing the canonical structures shows the negative charge appearing specifically at the **ortho and para** carbons, so it is these positions that are electron rich and attract the electrophile. Correspondingly, when the electrophile attacks ortho or para the arenium ion has an extra canonical structure in which the oxygen lone pair gives the electron-deficient carbon a complete octet — the most stable contributor of all. No such structure is possible for meta attack, so the meta product is much less favoured.

In practice the para product predominates over the ortho, because the ortho positions are sterically crowded by the alkoxy group — hence the 90% yield of \(p\)-bromoanisole.

**Step 1 — protonation of the ether.** HI is sufficiently acidic to protonate the ether oxygen, converting the poor leaving group \(-\text{OR}\) into the good one, an alcohol:
\(\text{CH}_3-\ddot{\text{O}}-\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}-\text{I} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{O}}(\text{H})-\text{CH}_3 + \text{I}^-\)

**Step 2 — \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) attack by iodide.** Iodide is a good nucleophile; it attacks one of the methyl carbons from the side opposite the leaving group, and methanol departs:
\(\text{I}^- + \text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{O}}(\text{H})-\text{CH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{I} + \text{CH}_3\text{OH}\)

Both groups are methyl, so it does not matter which carbon is attacked. If HI is in excess and the mixture is heated, the methanol formed is protonated in turn and converted to a second molecule of iodomethane:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{OH} + \text{HI} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{I} + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

The reaction is \(\text{S}_\text{N}2\) because a methyl carbon is unhindered and a methyl carbocation would be far too unstable to form.

The methoxy group of anisole is activating and ortho, para directing, so every one of these electrophilic substitutions gives the ortho and para products, the para predominating for steric reasons.

(i) **Friedel-Crafts alkylation:**
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OCH}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{Cl} \xrightarrow[\text{CS}_2]{\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3} \) 2-methoxytoluene (minor) + 4-methoxytoluene (major) \(+\ \text{HCl}\)

(ii) **Nitration:**
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OCH}_3 \xrightarrow[\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4]{\text{conc. HNO}_3}\) 2-nitroanisole (minor) + 4-nitroanisole (major) \(+\ \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(iii) **Bromination in ethanoic acid:**
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OCH}_3 + \text{Br}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}}\) o-bromoanisole (minor) + p-bromoanisole (major, about 90%) \(+\ \text{HBr}\)
No iron(III) bromide is needed, because the methoxy group activates the ring strongly enough to polarise the bromine molecule itself.

(iv) **Friedel-Crafts acetylation:**
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OCH}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{COCl} \xrightarrow{\text{anhyd. AlCl}_3}\) 2-methoxyacetophenone (minor) + 4-methoxyacetophenone (major) \(+\ \text{HCl}\)

Each alcohol is made by acid-catalysed hydration of an alkene. Markovnikov's rule fixes which alkene is needed: the \(-\text{OH}\) must end up on the carbon that becomes the more stable carbocation, so the double bond is placed between the carbinol carbon and one of its neighbours.

(i) 1-Methylcyclohexan-1-ol, from **1-methylcyclohexene** — protonation of the ring carbon next to the substituted one gives the tertiary carbocation, and water attacks the carbon bearing the methyl group.

(ii) 4-Methylheptan-4-ol, from **4-methylhept-3-ene**, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) — the proton adds to C-3 and the tertiary carbocation forms at C-4.

(iii) Pentan-2-ol, from **pent-1-ene**, \(\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) — the proton adds to the terminal \(\text{CH}_2\), giving the secondary carbocation at C-2 (pent-2-ene would serve equally well).

(iv) 2-Cyclohexylbutan-2-ol, from **2-cyclohexylbut-2-ene**, \(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}-\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_3\) — the proton adds to C-3 and the tertiary carbocation forms at C-2, which then takes the \(-\text{OH}\).

In each case the reagent is water in the presence of dilute acid, \(\text{H}_2\text{O}/\text{H}^+\).

The reaction goes through a carbocation which rearranges, which is why the bromine ends up on a carbon that did not carry the \(-\text{OH}\) group.

**Step 1 — protonation of the alcohol.** The oxygen lone pair takes up a proton from HBr, making water the leaving group:
\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\text{OH})-\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}^+ \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}(\overset{+}{\text{O}}\text{H}_2)-\text{CH}_3\)

**Step 2 — loss of water.** A secondary carbocation is formed at C-2:
\(\text{CH}_3-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)-\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{H}-\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

**Step 3 — 1,2-hydride shift.** The hydrogen on C-3, together with its bonding pair, migrates to the positive C-2. This converts the secondary carbocation into the appreciably more stable **tertiary** carbocation, in which the charge is relieved by the \(+I\) effect and hyperconjugation of three alkyl groups:
\(\text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{C}}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\)

**Step 4 — capture by bromide.** The nucleophile attacks the tertiary carbon:
\(\text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{C}}(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3 + \text{Br}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3-\text{C}(\text{Br})(\text{CH}_3)-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_3\)

The product is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, as shown in the question.
